triage.name: Carotid Artery Disease
triage.reason: Often asymptomatic but can present with TIA or amaurosis fugax; history, exam, and vascular imaging make a solid stroke-prevention case.

demographics: More common with increasing age; prevalence rises steeply after age 65
Men are affected somewhat more often than women, though the gap narrows with age
More common in Black and Hispanic populations, largely reflecting higher rates of hypertension and diabetes

risk_factors.text: Cigarette smoking or history of smoking
Established atherosclerotic disease elsewhere (coronary, peripheral, aortic)
Family history of premature cardiovascular disease
Elevated homocysteine or other thrombophilic states

family_history: Premature coronary or carotid artery disease in a first-degree relative
Stroke in a parent or sibling
exposures: Neck radiation therapy (for head and neck cancer)

chief_complaints.text: My doctor heard a whooshing sound in my neck
I suddenly couldn't see out of one eye for a few minutes
My right arm and leg went weak and numb for a little while
I couldn't get my words out properly for a few minutes
The side of my face drooped for a short time

hpi.onset: Often no symptoms at all; when symptoms occur they come on suddenly, out of the blue, and are maximal within seconds to a minute
hpi.duration: Episodes typically last a few minutes and resolve within an hour; a completed stroke leaves deficits that persist beyond 24 hours
hpi.progression: Asymptomatic narrowing may be found incidentally and progress silently over years; symptomatic episodes may be single or recurrent, and a TIA can be followed days to weeks later by a stroke
hpi.location: Symptoms reflect the opposite side of the body from the affected artery; the eye on the same side as the narrowed artery is typically involved
hpi.quality: Sudden loss of vision in one eye described as a shade coming down, or sudden weakness, numbness, or clumsiness of one arm, leg, or side of the face
hpi.severity: Highly variable; TIA symptoms are frightening but fully resolve, while a stroke leaves fixed deficits
hpi.timing: Abrupt onset, no warning, often at rest or on waking; episodes are brief and self-limited

associated_symptoms.text: Sudden weakness or clumsiness of one arm or leg
Sudden numbness or tingling of the face, arm, or leg on one side
Sudden loss of vision or a dark curtain over one eye (amaurosis fugax)
Slurred speech or trouble finding words
Drooping of one side of the face
Sudden dizziness, unsteadiness, or trouble walking
Severe headache at the onset of a stroke

pertinent_negatives: Gradual, stepwise, or fluctuating weakness over hours to days
Symptoms in both arms and legs simultaneously
Isolated vertigo without other brainstem symptoms
Symptoms that worsen with neck movement or position

positives.text: Transient weakness or numbness of one side of the body

argues_against: Symptoms in multiple vascular territories at once

positives.text: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye lasting minutes
Blurred or dim vision in one eye
Whooshing sound heard by the doctor in the neck
Chest pain or pressure on exertion

argues_against: Known atrial fibrillation with irregular pulse

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms may be attributed to aging or arthritis; a TIA can present as confusion, unsteadiness, or a fall rather than clear weakness or vision loss.
Neuropathy and prior small-vessel disease can mask or mimic symptoms, and episodes may be dismissed as low blood sugar.
missing_classic_features: Sudden focal deficit clearly distinct from baseline

atypical.how_it_differs: Carotid disease in children is rare and usually related to trauma, dissection, radiation, or a hypercoagulable state rather than atherosclerosis; presentation is stroke or TIA without vascular risk factors.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; often completely asymptomatic
general.moderate: Comfortable at rest; may have residual mild focal deficit from a prior TIA or stroke
general.severe: May appear anxious or have a visible focal neurologic deficit (facial droop, arm drift, gait instability)
general.critical: Acutely ill, may be confused, aphasic, or have dense hemiparesis; requires urgent stroke evaluation

findings.maneuver: Auscultate over the common, internal, and external carotid arteries bilaterally with the bell of the stethoscope while the patient holds their breath
findings.finding: A focal, high-pitched systolic bruit over the mid-to-upper neck (over the carotid bifurcation), which may radiate to the jaw or mastoid

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the neck when a bruit is expected but not heard
findings.finding: Absence of a bruit despite known or suspected disease; a very tight stenosis or near-occlusion may be silent

findings.maneuver: Palpate the common carotid artery medial to the sternocleidomastoid at the level of the thyroid cartilage, one side at a time
findings.finding: Diminished or asymmetric carotid pulse on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to smile and show their teeth
findings.finding: Unilateral lower facial weakness (nasolabial fold flattening, asymmetric smile)

findings.maneuver: Have the patient hold both arms out with eyes closed for 10 seconds
findings.finding: Pronator drift or downward drift of one arm

findings.maneuver: Test strength in all four extremities (grip, wrist extension, hip flexion, dorsiflexion) and compare sides
findings.finding: Unilateral weakness or clumsiness of the arm, leg, or face

findings.maneuver: Test light touch, pinprick, and proprioception in all extremities
findings.finding: Unilateral sensory loss or extinction on double simultaneous stimulation

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to repeat a phrase, name objects, and follow a simple command
findings.finding: Slurred speech (dysarthria) or difficulty with word finding, comprehension, or repetition (aphasia)

findings.maneuver: Confrontational visual field testing in all four quadrants
findings.finding: Homonymous visual field cut or unilateral visual loss consistent with retinal ischemia

findings.maneuver: Perform a dilated fundoscopic exam of both eyes
findings.finding: Hollenhorst plaques (bright, refractile cholesterol emboli at retinal arteriolar bifurcations) or retinal pallor

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the neck in a patient with non-vascular causes of dizziness or syncope
findings.finding: No carotid bruit; symmetric carotid pulses

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and palpate the radial pulse for rate and regularity
findings.finding: Regular rate and rhythm without murmur, rub, or gallop; no evidence of atrial fibrillation or valvular source of emboli

findings.maneuver: Complete a focused neurologic exam including cranial nerves, motor, sensory, coordination, and gait
findings.finding: No focal neurologic deficit; normal speech, visual fields, and strength

findings.maneuver: Palpate the posterior neck and percuss the spinous processes
findings.finding: No neck tenderness, stiffness, or meningismus

labs.caveat: Fasting lipid panel; hypercholesterolemia is a modifiable risk factor and guides statin therapy.
Primary target for lipid-lowering therapy; very high values suggest familial hypercholesterolemia.
Low HDL is an independent cardiovascular risk factor.
Screens for prediabetes and diabetes, both strong risk factors for carotid atherosclerosis.
Baseline renal function before contrast-enhanced imaging or revascularization; chronic kidney disease is a risk factor.
Anemia is not caused by carotid disease but may worsen cerebral ischemia and is checked before surgery.
Relevant before carotid endarterectomy and when antiplatelet therapy is planned.
Checked before surgery; a prolonged INR raises bleeding risk with endarterectomy.
Thyroid disease can cause atrial fibrillation, an alternative embolic source for stroke.

findings.finding: Atrial fibrillation with irregularly irregular ventricular response
ST depression or T-wave inversion in a coronary distribution suggesting concomitant coronary artery disease
Pathologic Q waves from a prior myocardial infarction
Left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria from chronic hypertension

imaging.preferred_when: First-line screening and diagnostic test; no radiation or contrast

findings.text: Focal plaque at the carotid bifurcation with increased peak systolic velocity in the internal carotid artery
Elevated internal carotid to common carotid peak systolic velocity ratio consistent with stenosis
Plaque described as heterogeneous or echolucent, suggesting a lipid-rich unstable plaque
Near-occlusion or complete occlusion with absent or reversed flow
Turbulent flow and spectral broadening at the stenosis

imaging.study: CT angiography of the head and neck with contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When duplex is equivocal or discordant with symptoms, or when planning revascularization

findings.text: Focal luminal narrowing at the carotid bifurcation with calcified and noncalcified plaque
Percent stenosis measured by NASCET-style criteria
Ulcerated plaque surface
Tandem intracranial atherosclerotic disease
Carotid dissection with a mural hematoma or intimal flap

imaging.study: Magnetic resonance angiography of the neck
imaging.preferred_when: Patients who cannot receive iodinated contrast or when plaque composition is of interest

findings.text: Flow-related signal loss at the site of stenosis
Plaque with a thin or ruptured fibrous cap on high-resolution sequences
Intraplaque hemorrhage

imaging.preferred_when: Rarely needed; reserved for discordant noninvasive studies or as part of an endovascular procedure

findings.text: Direct measurement of the residual lumen at the carotid bifurcation
Ulcerated or irregular plaque contour

imaging.study: MRI of the brain without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When a TIA or stroke is suspected, to define the infarct and exclude mimics

findings.text: Diffusion restriction in a cortical or deep border-zone territory consistent with acute infarction
No acute infarct in a pure TIA
Old lacunar or cortical infarcts from prior events
White matter chronic microvascular changes

imaging.study: CT of the head without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Initial emergency evaluation of a suspected acute stroke to exclude hemorrhage

findings.text: No acute hemorrhage
Hypodensity in a vascular territory if infarction is established
Old infarct or chronic white matter hypodensity

imaging.preferred_when: When a cardioembolic source is suspected in a patient with TIA or stroke

findings.text: Normal study with no intracardiac thrombus or valve vegetation
Left atrial enlargement or spontaneous echo contrast suggesting atrial fibrillation
Left ventricular thrombus or reduced ejection fraction
Aortic or mitral valve calcification or vegetation

initial.why: First-line test to detect and grade carotid stenosis in a patient with a bruit, TIA, or amaurosis fugax
initial.only_if: First-line test to detect and grade carotid stenosis in a patient with a bruit, TIA, or amaurosis fugax

initial.why: Identifies hyperlipidemia and guides statin therapy
Screens for diabetes, a major modifiable risk factor
Baseline renal function and electrolytes before contrast imaging or surgery
Baseline blood counts before antiplatelet therapy or endarterectomy
Baseline coagulation studies before any planned revascularization
Looks for atrial fibrillation or coronary disease as an alternative or coexisting cause of stroke

initial.test: CT of the head without contrast
initial.why: Excludes hemorrhage in a patient with acute focal neurologic symptoms
initial.only_if: acute stroke or TIA symptoms are present

initial.test: MRI of the brain without contrast
initial.why: Defines the infarct and distinguishes TIA from stroke
initial.only_if: TIA or stroke is suspected and the patient is stable

confirmatory.test: CT angiography of the head and neck with contrast
confirmatory.why: Confirms and quantifies stenosis when duplex is equivocal or when revascularization is being planned
confirmatory.only_if: Confirms and quantifies stenosis when duplex is equivocal or when revascularization is being planned

confirmatory.test: Magnetic resonance angiography of the neck
confirmatory.why: Alternative confirmatory study when iodinated contrast is contraindicated
confirmatory.only_if: contrast allergy or severe renal impairment

confirmatory.why: Gold standard for stenosis measurement when noninvasive studies are discordant
confirmatory.only_if: noninvasive studies disagree or endovascular treatment is planned

supporting.why: Screens for a cardioembolic source such as atrial fibrillation, thrombus, or valve disease
supporting.only_if: TIA or stroke has occurred and no clear carotid source is found

supporting.why: Thyroid dysfunction can cause atrial fibrillation and embolic stroke
Very high values raise concern for giant cell arteritis or another inflammatory vasculopathy
supporting.only_if: headache, jaw claudication, or systemic symptoms are present

not_indicated.why: Not useful for diagnosing carotid atherosclerosis
Does not help identify or grade carotid stenosis
No role in the evaluation of carotid disease
Not relevant to neck or neurologic symptoms
Does not contribute to the diagnosis of carotid artery disease
Not indicated unless infection or subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected
Screening asymptomatic average-risk adults is not recommended; reserve for symptomatic patients or those with a bruit
not_indicated.only_if: asymptomatic screening in a patient without a bruit or vascular risk factors

not_indicated.test: CT angiography of the head and neck with contrast
not_indicated.why: Not a first-line test; exposes the patient to contrast and radiation without adding to a clear duplex result
not_indicated.only_if: duplex is equivocal or revascularization is planned

decision_points: Distinguish TIA from stroke by duration of symptoms and imaging findings; both require urgent evaluation
Confirm and quantify stenosis with a second study before recommending revascularization
Assess renal function before contrast-enhanced CT angiography
Consider atrial fibrillation and other cardioembolic sources when carotid disease does not explain the symptoms
Symptomatic high-grade stenosis is a vascular emergency; involve vascular surgery early

criteria.name: Symptomatic carotid stenosis
criteria.summary: Focal neurologic symptoms (TIA, amaurosis fugax, or stroke) in the territory of the affected carotid artery within the preceding six months, with imaging confirming stenosis.
items: Ipsilateral focal neurologic deficit or transient monocular visual loss
Symptoms attributable to the carotid territory
Stenosis confirmed on duplex ultrasound or angiography

criteria.name: Asymptomatic carotid stenosis
criteria.summary: Carotid bruit or incidental imaging finding of stenosis in a patient with no recent ipsilateral neurologic symptoms.
items: No TIA, amaurosis fugax, or stroke in the preceding six months
Stenosis detected on duplex ultrasound or other vascular imaging

differential.name: Cardioembolic stroke from atrial fibrillation
differential.why_considered: Sudden focal neurologic deficit or transient monocular visual loss in an older adult with vascular risk factors; embolic strokes can mimic carotid territory ischemia.
differential.trigger: Irregularly irregular pulse or known atrial fibrillation in a patient with a sudden focal deficit

history: Palpitations or known atrial fibrillation
Symptoms may occur in multiple vascular territories or at different times
No preceding neck bruit or amaurosis fugax
exam: Focal deficit may be cortical (aphasia, neglect) rather than purely motor
labs: Normal lipid panel does not exclude cardioembolic source
imaging: Carotid duplex shows no significant stenosis
Brain MRI shows infarcts in multiple territories or a cortical wedge
Echocardiogram may show left atrial enlargement, spontaneous echo contrast, or thrombus
ecg: Atrial fibrillation with irregularly irregular ventricular response

differential.name: Lacunar stroke from small vessel disease
differential.why_considered: Sudden focal weakness or sensory loss in a patient with hypertension or diabetes; small vessel disease is a common cause of stroke and can resemble carotid territory ischemia.
differential.trigger: Pure motor or pure sensory deficit without cortical signs in a patient with long-standing hypertension

history: Long-standing hypertension or diabetes
No amaurosis fugax or neck bruit
Deficit may be purely motor or purely sensory
exam: No aphasia, neglect, or visual field cut
Normal fundoscopic exam without Hollenhorst plaques
labs: Renal function may show chronic kidney disease
imaging: Carotid duplex shows no significant stenosis
Brain MRI shows a small deep infarct in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, or internal capsule

differential.name: Giant cell arteritis
differential.why_considered: Older adult with sudden visual loss or transient visual symptoms; cranial arteritis can cause amaurosis fugax or stroke and is a treatable emergency.
differential.trigger: New headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or elevated inflammatory markers in an older adult with visual symptoms

history: New-onset headache, often temporal
Jaw claudication or scalp tenderness
Polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms (shoulder or hip girdle pain, morning stiffness)
Visual loss may be permanent rather than transient
exam: Tender, nodular, or pulseless temporal artery
Fundoscopic exam may show pale, swollen optic disc
labs: Anemia and thrombocytosis may be present
imaging: Temporal artery biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with giant cells
Carotid duplex may show halo sign in temporal arteries but no bifurcation plaque

differential.name: Carotid artery dissection
differential.why_considered: Younger patient with sudden neck pain, headache, and focal neurologic symptoms; dissection is a non-atherosclerotic cause of carotid territory ischemia.
differential.trigger: Neck pain or headache with Horner syndrome or focal deficit after neck trauma or manipulation

history: Recent neck trauma, chiropractic manipulation, or strenuous activity
Ipsilateral neck pain, headache, or facial pain
Younger age without traditional atherosclerotic risk factors
exam: Partial Horner syndrome (ptosis and miosis without anhidrosis)
Cranial nerve palsy (especially lower cranial nerves)
labs: Coagulation studies may show hypercoagulable state
imaging: CT or MR angiography shows a tapered flame-like occlusion, intimal flap, or mural hematoma
Carotid duplex may show abnormal flow but is less sensitive for dissection

differential.name: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency
differential.why_considered: Dizziness, unsteadiness, or visual symptoms in an older adult with vascular risk factors; posterior circulation ischemia can be mistaken for carotid disease.

history: Vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, or ataxia
Symptoms often bilateral or crossing sides
No amaurosis fugax
exam: Nystagmus, gait ataxia, or cranial nerve findings
Visual field deficits may be homonymous hemianopsia
imaging: CT or MR angiography shows stenosis or occlusion in vertebral or basilar arteries
Brain MRI shows infarct in posterior circulation territory

differential.name: Vasovagal syncope
differential.why_considered: Transient loss of consciousness or near-syncope can be confused with TIA, especially in older adults.

history: Prodrome of warmth, nausea, diaphoresis, or tunnel vision
Triggered by prolonged standing, pain, or emotional stress
No focal neurologic deficit after recovery

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: Sudden confusion, weakness, or visual disturbance in a patient with diabetes; hypoglycemia can mimic TIA.

history: Diabetes treated with insulin or sulfonylurea
Missed meal or excessive medication
Symptoms improve with glucose intake
labs: Resolution of symptoms with glucose correction

differential.name: Seizure with postictal Todd paralysis
differential.why_considered: Transient focal weakness after a seizure can be mistaken for TIA or stroke.

history: Witnessed convulsion or loss of consciousness
Tongue biting, incontinence, or confusion after event
No amaurosis fugax
exam: Focal weakness that resolves over hours
imaging: Brain MRI may show structural lesion or normal

severity.mild: Asymptomatic carotid bruit or incidental finding of less than 50% stenosis; no recent TIA or stroke; well-controlled risk factors
severity.moderate: Asymptomatic stenosis of 50–69% or symptomatic stenosis of less than 50%; may have remote history of TIA; risk factors partially controlled
severity.severe: Symptomatic high-grade stenosis (70–99%) or asymptomatic stenosis of 70% or greater; recent TIA, amaurosis fugax, or minor stroke; requires urgent vascular evaluation
severity.critical: Acute ischemic stroke with fluctuating or progressive neurologic deficit, near-occlusion, or stroke in evolution; requires emergent stroke team evaluation and consideration of revascularization

red_flags.finding: Sudden focal neurologic deficit (face, arm, leg weakness or numbness)
red_flags.meaning: Acute stroke or TIA; activate stroke pathway immediately
Retinal ischemia from carotid embolus; high risk of subsequent stroke

red_flags.finding: New carotid bruit with recent TIA symptoms
red_flags.meaning: Symptomatic carotid stenosis; urgent vascular imaging and surgical consultation
Impending stroke; requires emergent evaluation and possible revascularization

red_flags.finding: Altered level of consciousness or dense hemiparesis
red_flags.meaning: Large territory stroke; risk of herniation and life-threatening edema

complications.name: Transient ischemic attack
clues: Sudden focal deficit lasting minutes to less than 24 hours

complications.name: Ischemic stroke
clues: May occur days to weeks after a TIA

complications.name: Amaurosis fugax
clues: Described as a shade coming down

complications.name: Carotid occlusion
clues: Progression of stenosis to complete blockage
May be asymptomatic or cause large stroke

complications.name: Plaque rupture with embolization
clues: Ulcerated or echolucent plaque on imaging

special_populations.differences: Symptoms may be attributed to aging or arthritis; TIA can present as confusion, unsteadiness, or a fall rather than clear weakness or vision loss. Higher prevalence of asymptomatic stenosis and greater surgical risk.
Neuropathy and prior small-vessel disease can mask or mimic symptoms; episodes may be dismissed as hypoglycemia. Higher risk of restenosis after revascularization.
Carotid disease is rare in pregnancy; when it occurs, consider dissection, hypercoagulable states, or preeclampsia. Management must balance fetal safety with maternal stroke prevention.

Carotid disease in children is rare and usually related to trauma, dissection, radiation, or a hypercoagulable state rather than atherosclerosis; presentation is stroke or TIA without vascular risk factors.

key_questions.question: Have you had any sudden weakness, numbness, or clumsiness on one side of your body, even if it went away?
key_questions.looking_for: Transient or persistent focal neurologic deficit in a carotid territory; establishes whether the stenosis is symptomatic

key_questions.question: Have you had any sudden loss of vision in one eye, like a shade coming down, that then cleared?
key_questions.looking_for: Amaurosis fugax, a classic embolic symptom of ipsilateral carotid disease

key_questions.question: How long did those symptoms last, and are they completely gone now?
key_questions.looking_for: Under an hour with full resolution suggests TIA; persistent deficit beyond 24 hours suggests stroke

key_questions.question: Did the symptoms affect one side of your body or one eye only?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral, lateralizing symptoms consistent with a single carotid territory rather than diffuse or bilateral causes

key_questions.question: Have these episodes happened more than once, or are they getting more frequent or severe?
key_questions.looking_for: Crescendo TIAs, which signal impending stroke and the need for urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Did you have any trouble speaking, finding words, or understanding what others said?
key_questions.looking_for: Aphasia or dysarthria, supporting a left carotid territory event

key_questions.question: Has anyone ever told you they heard a whooshing sound or murmur in your neck?
key_questions.looking_for: A known carotid bruit, which may be the only clue in asymptomatic disease

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or diabetes, and are they treated?
key_questions.looking_for: Major modifiable atherosclerotic risk factors and how well they are controlled

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a heart attack, leg artery disease, or a stroke before?
key_questions.looking_for: Established atherosclerotic disease elsewhere, which raises the likelihood of carotid involvement

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or have you smoked in the past? How much and for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former tobacco use, one of the strongest risk factors for carotid atherosclerosis

key_questions.question: Do you have any palpitations or a known irregular heartbeat?
key_questions.looking_for: Atrial fibrillation, an alternative embolic source that can mimic carotid disease

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had a stroke, heart attack, or artery disease at a young age?
key_questions.looking_for: Premature cardiovascular disease in a first-degree relative, supporting a genetic predisposition

key_questions.question: Have you ever had radiation treatment to your neck or head?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior neck radiation, which accelerates carotid atherosclerosis

key_questions.question: Are you having any weakness, numbness, or vision loss right now?
key_questions.looking_for: An acute ongoing stroke, which requires immediate activation of the stroke pathway

reasoning_points: Sudden, focal, unilateral neurologic symptoms or transient monocular visual loss in a patient with vascular risk factors
Symptoms lasting minutes to under an hour with full resolution suggest TIA; persistent deficits suggest stroke
Carotid bruit on auscultation over the bifurcation supports the diagnosis but its absence does not exclude severe stenosis
Atherosclerotic risk factors such as hypertension, smoking, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and older age
Carotid duplex ultrasound showing focal plaque and elevated peak systolic velocity at the bifurcation
Confirmation and quantification of stenosis with CT or MR angiography when duplex is equivocal or revascularization is planned
Exclusion of alternative embolic sources such as atrial fibrillation, and of mimics such as lacunar stroke, dissection, or giant cell arteritis
Distinction between symptomatic and asymptomatic stenosis, because it drives the urgency and choice of revascularization

easy: Older adult with hypertension and smoking history
Classic amaurosis fugax described as a shade coming down over one eye
Carotid duplex shows high-grade stenosis at the bifurcation
medium: Asymptomatic patient with an incidental carotid bruit found on routine exam
Transient arm and face weakness that resolved before arrival, with a normal neurologic exam
Patient with both carotid disease and atrial fibrillation, requiring determination of the true embolic source
Very tight stenosis with no audible bruit
hard: Older adult whose TIA presented as confusion, unsteadiness, or a fall rather than clear weakness
Patient with diabetes whose symptoms were dismissed as hypoglycemia
Younger patient with neck pain and focal deficit due to carotid dissection rather than atherosclerosis
Patient with a pure motor lacunar syndrome and no cortical signs, mimicking carotid territory ischemia
Older adult with visual loss and headache due to giant cell arteritis rather than carotid emboli
